newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - CSR sees another profit slump.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CSR sees another profit slump.

text.p: CSR Ltd on Monday prepared shareholders for a second successive fall in annual net profit, blaming its problems on the weak Australian economy and wishing it had more assets invested in the United States.

With major operations in housing, aluminium, sugar, and timber, CSR said net profit in the first six months to September 30 fell 24 percent to A$154.7 million and predicted lower second half earnings and a likely fall in second half dividend.
At a briefing for analysts, who had been forewarned of the first half slump, managing director Geoff Kells said the company was working hard to ensure that profits soon recovered.
Some shareholders bailed out of CSR stock on Monday rather than wait for the corporate turnaround, with its shares ending 10 cents lower at A$4.18 on turnover of 2.59 million.
A number of analysts said they would take another look at their 1996/97 net profit estimates following the company's comments on the outlook and its first half performance.

Hit hard by a downturn in the Australian housing market which was partly offset by strong performances from CSR America and aluminium, CSR reported an 18 percent fall in 1995/96 net profit (April-March) to A$320.1 million. This time around, only CSR America was performing up to expectations, Kells said.
Of the six divisions, only the U.S. and sugar increased net profit in the latest half.
While Kells was concerned about the outlook for raw and refined sugar prices, he was confident that the U.S. division would continue to grow, particularly in Florida and Las Vegas.
Pointing to a chart of the ever-increasing profit rise from the U.S., Kells said: "This one here I would like to linger on as long as I possibly can."
"There is a fairly bullish result in America and as far as we can see, while the market is a bit toppy, we don't as yet see any fall-off in it."
CSR America provided more than half of the net profit in the latest six months, with a 13 percent rise to A$78.5 million, and without currency factors the rise would have been 20 percent.

Kells said CSR achieved higher volumes, prices and margins from Florida -- key financial parameters it could not meet from its Australian operations -- and growth in other U.S. markets such as polyethylene pipe and quarrying.

CSR West was heavily focussed on the desert city of Las Vegas. "You could almost call it (the division) CSR Las Vegas these days. Las Vegas is a boom town for us where both quarry and concrete volumes have been very good indeed," he said.

CSR was not merely waiting for a recovery in the Australian economy and a pickup in the local housing market, Kells said, and had introduced "internal efficiencies" such as a focus on price rather than market share and a cutback in capital expenditure.

The company also expected to ratchet up its level of asset sales, which had already recovered A$139 million in recent months, with more than 50 plants up for sale in Australia and the United States, Kells said.
